questions.q: Well-defined layers interfaces allow changing the implementation of one layer with a completely different implementation without affecting the other layers.
questions.e: Layers talk only through their interfaces, so one layer's implementation can be replaced while its interface stays the same.

questions.q: Physical and data link are implemented in hardware in the network interface card (NIC)
questions.e: The NIC holds the physical and data link layers. The upper layers run in software.

questions.q: Semantics of protocol means structure or format of the data message, and their order.
questions.e: That describes syntax. Semantics is the meaning of each section of bits.

questions.q: National ISPs (Tier-2 ISPs) connect to each other at private peering points.
questions.e: National ISPs interconnect at IXPs (public peering). Private peering points are how international ISPs connect.

questions.q: Computer networks are the example of:
questions.e: Computers produce digital data and send it as digital signals, which is digital-to-digital conversion (line coding).

questions.q: The bit rate for the below signal is:
questions.e: Eight signal elements fit in one second and each carries log<sub>2</sub>4 = 2 bits, so the bit rate is 8 × 2 = 16 bps.

questions.q: Which statement is true about the figure below
o: It is a composite signal with single sine wave in it.
It is a composite signal with many sine waves in it
It is a composite signal with only digital signals in it.
questions.e: A composite signal is the sum of many sine waves. The ripple on each flat top shows the added harmonics.

questions.q: Figure below is example of Today's Telephone networks; choose the statement true about it.
o: Today's Telephone network is only using Digital transmission
Today's Telephone network is using combination of Analog and Digital transmissions
Today's Telephone network is only using Analog Transmission
questions.e: The local loop from modem to end office is analog. The codec at the end office converts it, and the trunk between offices is digital.

questions.q: Periodic Digital Signals are used mostly in Computer Data Communications.
questions.e: Data communication mostly uses nonperiodic digital signals, because real data does not repeat in a fixed pattern.

questions.q: Figure below explains the problem between sender and receiver computer which is:
questions.e: The receiver's clock runs faster, so 8 sent bits are read as 12. The bit intervals no longer line up, which is a synchronization problem.

questions.q: To separate one frame from another a ________ is added at the beginning and end of the frame.
questions.e: Framing marks each frame's start and end with a flag. Stuffing only protects flag patterns that appear inside the data.

questions.q: A2:34:45:11:92:F1 is ________ Physical address.
questions.e: Check the second hex digit from the left: 2 is even, so the last bit of the first byte is 0 and the address is unicast (Chapter 4 slides, even = unicast, odd = multicast). Multicast is the trap answer here.

questions.q: If the receiver using checksum technique gets result a non zero value, the receiver will discard that data word.
questions.e: The receiver accepts only when the checked result is zero. Any non-zero result means an error, so the data word is discarded.

questions.q: Reed-Solomon code used today for both detection and correction is a ____ code.
questions.e: Reed-Solomon is a cyclic code. Block code is the wider family, and a checksum detects errors only.

questions.q: The first address assigned to an organization in classless addressing ________.
o: must be fully divisible by the number of addresses
must belong to one of the A, B, or C classes
questions.e: A classless block must start on a boundary of its own size, so the first address is divisible by the number of addresses.

questions.q: What is the first address of a block of classless addresses if one of the addresses is 12.2.2.76/10?
questions.e: Keep the first 10 bits and zero the rest: 12.00000010… becomes 12.00000000.0.0, so 12.0.0.0.

questions.q: In a block, the mask in CIDR is /15; we can write the same as.
Identify the class of the following IPv4 address: <u>192</u>.1.2.3.
questions.e: A first byte from 192 to 223 is Class C.

questions.q: Routers in the path are not allowed to ________.
questions.e: Routers may fragment an IPv4 packet when it exceeds the next link's MTU. They never change the source or destination address. (c) follows the textbook rule; (b) is the closest alternative, since routers decapsulate only to fragment.

questions.q: What is true about Time to Live (TTL) field of IP header:
o: Router discards the packet when it value becomes 1.
Router discards the packet when it value becomes 0.
Router gives top priority to that packet when this field has 100.
questions.e: Each router decrements TTL. When it reaches 0 the packet is discarded, which stops it looping forever.

questions.q: Technique/s for sharing the transmission medium using channelization is/are:
questions.e: Channelization has three methods: FDMA, TDMA and CDMA.

questions.q: A company has 10 computers that need to be connected in a fully connected mesh topology. How many dedicated links are required?
questions.e: A fully connected mesh with 10 computers requires 10×9÷2 = 45 dedicated links.

questions.q: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for moving frames from one hop (node) to the next?
questions.e: The Data Link layer is responsible for node-to-node delivery of frames.

questions.q: A user wants to send a large file over the Internet. Which of the following correctly describes the flow of data from the user's application to the network cable?
o: Data → Application → Presentation → Session → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical
Data → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical
Data → Data Link → Network → Transport → Physical
Data → Network → Transport → Data Link → Physical
questions.e: The OSI data flow toward the medium passes through Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, and Physical layers.

questions.q: Scenario: Two computers are communicating. Computer A is sending data to Computer B. At the Transport layer of Computer A, a TCP header is added. When Computer B receives the data, which layer will read and process this TCP header?
o: Data Link layer of Computer B
questions.e: The Transport layer processes the TCP header at the receiving computer.

questions.q: Which type of network connection uses a dedicated link between exactly two devices?
questions.e: A point-to-point connection provides a dedicated link between exactly two devices.

questions.q: What is the PDU (Protocol Data Unit) called at the Network layer of the OSI model?
questions.e: Packet or datagram is the PDU associated with the Network layer.

questions.q: The physical layer is responsible for all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Representation of bits into electrical or optical signals
questions.e: Process-to-process delivery is a Transport layer responsibility, not a Physical layer responsibility.

questions.q: Scenario: You are downloading multiple files simultaneously from a web server. Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for keeping these different application data separate from each other?
questions.e: The Session layer is responsible for managing sessions and keeping different application activities logically separate.

questions.q: In the OSI model, which of the following layers is implemented in hardware (in the Network Interface Card)?
questions.e: The Physical and Data Link layers are implemented in the network interface hardware.

questions.q: If a CRC generator polynomial has a degree of r, how many zero bits are appended to the dataword during CRC encoding?
questions.e: The remainder has r bits, so r zeros are appended before dividing.

questions.q: What is Forward Error Correction (FEC)?
o: A technique to detect and correct a limited number of errors without needing retransmission.
An encryption standard for securing L2 frames.
A protocol requiring the sender to resend all corrupted data blocks automatically.
A mechanism for doubling physical link bandwidth capacity.
questions.e: FEC adds enough redundancy for the receiver to repair limited errors by itself, without retransmission.

questions.q: In p-persistent CSMA, what step does a station take when it finds the medium idle?
o: Sends a polling frame to the central coordinator.
Transmits immediately with probability 1 without waiting.
Transmits with probability p, OR waits one time slot with probability (1 - p) and then re-senses.
Waits a random exponential backoff time before sensing again.
questions.e: Transmitting with probability 1 is 1-persistent. p-persistent transmits with probability p, otherwise waits one slot and senses again.

questions.q: CSMA/CD is widely used in which network topology when a hub is deployed?
questions.e: Stations cabled to a hub form a physical star, and the hub makes them share one collision domain, so CSMA/CD applies.
Layers talk only through their interfaces, so one layer's implementation can be replaced while its interface stays the same.

questions.q: A company has a computer belonging to the "HR Department" located in a room full of "IT Department" computers. The HR computer needs to be on the same broadcast domain as other HR computers in a different building, but the company does not want to run new physical cables to separate the departments. What is the technology that can solve this issue?
o: VLANs physically move the HR computer to the IT room by changing the switch port wiring.
VLANs divide the physical LAN into logical LANs using software, allowing the HR computer to be grouped with other HR devices regardless of physical location.
VLANs require the HR computer to have two Network Interface Cards (NICs) to connect to both broadcast domains.
VLANs increase the collision domain size to include the entire building, allowing the HR computer to communicate with everyone.
questions.e: A VLAN groups stations by software configuration, not by where they are plugged in, so no recabling is needed. VLANs create broadcast domains; they don't move wiring, need two NICs or enlarge collision domains.

questions.q: A company places its HR and Sales departments in separate VLANs. What is one benefit?
o: Eliminating the need for IP addresses
Increasing the physical speed of their cables
questions.e: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, so HR broadcasts never reach Sales (less traffic, more security). VLANs don't encrypt, remove IP addressing or change cable speed.

questions.q: What is the primary function of Virtual LAN (VLAN) technology, and how does a switch manage device membership?
o: It groups computers physically, and switches use routing tables to map device locations.
It divides a physical LAN into logical LANs, and switches maintain a lookup table to determine which VLAN a machine belongs to.
It replaces physical switches with software routers that rely on dynamic IP allocation.
It combines multiple physical networks into a single physical segment without using lookup tables.
questions.e: VLAN = logical LANs on one physical LAN. The switch keeps a table mapping each port (or MAC) to its VLAN. Switches don't use routing tables.

questions.q: Eight computers connect to one switch: VLAN 10 (A, B, C), VLAN 20 (D, E, F), VLAN 30 (G, H).
o: 1 broadcast domain, because all computers are connected to the same physical switch.
3 broadcast domains, corresponding to VLAN 10, VLAN 20, and VLAN 30.
8 broadcast domains, because each computer operates in its own isolated domain.
4 broadcast domains, including a native management VLAN.
questions.e: One broadcast domain per VLAN: 3. Without VLANs the switch would be 1 broadcast domain. (8 would be the number of collision domains, one per port.)

questions.q: Eight computers connect to one switch: VLAN 10 (A, B, C), VLAN 20 (D, E, F), VLAN 30 (G, H).
o: All seven other computers (B, C, D, E, F, G, and H) connected to the switch.
Only computers D, E, and F, because they share the same physical port group.
Only computers B and C, since A's incoming port is excluded from flooding within VLAN 10.
No other computers, because Layer 2 switches drop all broadcast traffic by default.
questions.e: A broadcast is flooded only to ports in the same VLAN, and never back out the port it arrived on: B and C.

questions.q: Eight computers connect to one switch: VLAN 10 (A, B, C), VLAN 20 (D, E, F), VLAN 30 (G, H).
o: Yes, because both computers are plugged into the exact same physical switch.
Yes, provided that the switch ports are configured in trunking mode.
No, because A belongs to VLAN 10 while D belongs to VLAN 20, and Layer 2 switching keeps these VLANs separate.
No, unless both computers share the exact same MAC address table entry.
questions.e: Different VLANs = different broadcast domains. Traffic between them needs a router (layer 3). A trunk only carries several VLANs between switches; it doesn't join them.

questions.q: A network administrator is manually configuring a new desktop computer to connect to the corporate network. The administrator inputs the IP Address 172.16.5.20 and the Subnet Mask 255.255.0.0. However, the computer cannot access the internet, only local network resources. Which crucial piece of information did the administrator likely forget to configure?
o: The MAC address of the switch port.
The VLAN ID for the department.
questions.e: Local traffic works with an IP and mask alone. Anything outside the network must go to the router, the default gateway. Without it the host has nowhere to send off-network packets.

questions.q: When a client requests an IP configuration from a DHCP server, which database does the server check first before selecting an address from the dynamic pool?
questions.e: A DHCP server has a static database (fixed physical-to-IP bindings) and a dynamic pool. It checks the static database first; only if the client isn't there does it lease a temporary address from the pool.

questions.q: Why does a NAT-enabled border router inherently provide basic firewall protection for devices on an internal network?
o: NAT automatically strips and drops all incoming UDP protocol packets at the interface.
Internal private IP addresses are fully encrypted before leaving the local subnet.
External hosts cannot initiate connections to an internal machine unless an internal machine initiates the communication session first.
NAT converts all incoming external packets into local ARP broadcast messages.
questions.e: The translation table only gets an entry when an inside host sends first. An unsolicited packet from outside matches no entry, so the router can't tell which private host it is for and drops it. NAT doesn't encrypt or drop UDP.

questions.q: Which network criterion covers the frequency of failures and the time a network takes to recover?
questions.e: Reliability is measured by how often failures happen, the recovery time and robustness in a catastrophe.

questions.q: True or false: Throughput and delay are both performance measures, and raising throughput usually increases delay.
questions.e: More throughput means more traffic in the network, which increases queuing, so the two often conflict.

questions.q: A link shared by more than two devices is a…
questions.e: Multipoint links are shared by several devices; point-to-point links connect exactly two.

questions.q: In which topology does one broken cable in the main backbone stop the whole network?
questions.e: Every device taps the single bus backbone, so a break in it disconnects everyone.

questions.q: Which topology gives privacy, robustness and easy fault isolation but needs the most cabling?
questions.e: Dedicated links between every pair of devices: robust and private, but expensive.

questions.q: True or false: In a star topology, if the hub fails the whole network fails.
questions.e: Every link goes through the hub.

questions.q: STC and Mobily are examples of which ISP level?
questions.e: National ISPs are tier 2; Sprint and AT&T are tier 1 backbones.

questions.q: True or false: National (tier 2) ISPs connect to each other at private peering points.
questions.e: National ISPs meet at Internet Exchange Points (public peering). Private peering points join international ISPs.

questions.q: Which organization creates standards for LANs and MANs (802.x)?
questions.e: IEEE 802 covers LANs and MANs.

questions.q: True or false: Well-defined interfaces let one layer's implementation be replaced without affecting the other layers.
questions.e: Layers only use the services of the layer below through its interface.

questions.q: True or false: The physical and data link layers are implemented in hardware on the network interface card.
questions.e: The NIC holds layers 1 and 2; upper layers run in software.

questions.q: Peer-to-peer communication between layers means that…
o: Each layer talks directly to the same layer on the other machine through headers
Layers skip the layers below them
questions.e: Logically, layer n on one machine communicates with layer n on the other, using the headers it adds.

questions.q: True or false: During encapsulation every layer adds a header, and the data link layer usually adds a trailer too.
questions.e: The trailer carries the error-detection field (for example the CRC).

questions.q: Which delivery is the network layer responsible for?
questions.e: Data link = hop to hop, network = host to host, transport = process to process.

questions.q: True or false: OSI has seven layers while the original TCP/IP suite has five, because session and presentation are folded into the application layer.
questions.e: TCP/IP merges session and presentation into application.

questions.q: True or false: A composite signal is made of many simple sine waves with different frequencies.
questions.e: A simple signal is one sine wave; a composite signal is a sum of many.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of digital transmission?
o: Signals can be regenerated by repeaters, so noise does not build up
questions.e: Repeaters regenerate the bits, removing noise instead of amplifying it.

questions.q: Attenuation of a digital signal is fixed with…
o: A repeater that regenerates the signal
questions.e: Analog signals use amplifiers; digital signals use repeaters.

questions.q: True or false: Doubling the bandwidth halves the propagation time.
questions.e: Bandwidth changes the transmission time; propagation depends only on distance and speed.

questions.q: Which UTP category supports 10 Gbps and 500 MHz?
questions.e: CAT6a: 500 MHz, 10 Gbps.

questions.q: Which is NOT a data link layer service?
questions.e: Routing belongs to the network layer. Data link: framing, addressing, flow control, error control, media access.

questions.q: True or false: The data link layer delivers frames only across one link (node to node), not across the whole Internet.
questions.e: It works hop by hop; the network layer handles end-to-end delivery.

questions.q: The flag 01111110 marks frame boundaries in…
questions.e: Bit-oriented protocols use the 01111110 flag and bit stuffing.

questions.q: True or false: A simple parity check can detect and correct a single-bit error.
questions.e: Parity only detects an odd number of errors; it cannot locate or correct them.

questions.q: The receiver divides the received codeword by the generator. It accepts the frame when…
questions.e: A zero remainder means no error was detected.

questions.q: True or false: A generator of degree r detects every burst error of length r or less.
questions.e: That is the burst-detection property of CRC.

questions.q: At the receiver, the one's-complement sum of all words including the checksum is all 1s. The packet is…
questions.e: All 1s (whose complement is 0) means no error detected.

questions.q: Which method is better for real-time multimedia where retransmission is too slow?
questions.e: FEC repairs data at the receiver without waiting for a resend.

questions.q: True or false: In Stop-and-Wait, the sender sends one frame and waits for its acknowledgment before sending the next.
questions.e: That is the whole protocol; it is simple but uses the link poorly on long delays.

questions.q: In CSMA, the vulnerable time equals…
questions.e: A station that starts within one propagation time cannot yet hear the other signal.

questions.q: True or false: Ethernet is the dominant wired LAN technology and is standardized as IEEE 802.3.
questions.e: Ethernet = IEEE 802.3.

questions.q: The SFD byte 10101011 tells the receiver that…
o: The next field is the destination address
questions.e: The start frame delimiter's final 11 marks the end of synchronization.

questions.q: True or false: A type/length value of 0x0800 is a type (IPv4) because it is at least 1536.
questions.e: Values ≥ 0x0600 (1536) are types; values ≤ 1500 are lengths.

questions.q: True or false: A source MAC address can be a multicast address.
questions.e: The source is always unicast.

questions.q: Which is NOT needed for full-duplex Ethernet?
o: A switch instead of a hub
questions.e: With dedicated full-duplex links there are no collisions, so CSMA/CD is turned off.

questions.q: True or false: Half-duplex Ethernet (hub or shared medium) uses CSMA/CD.
questions.e: Stations share the medium, so collisions are possible and must be detected.

questions.q: Why does Ethernet have a minimum frame length of 64 bytes?
o: So a sender is still transmitting when a collision comes back, letting CSMA/CD detect it
questions.e: A frame shorter than the round-trip collision window could finish before the collision is heard.

questions.q: True or false: A hub filters frames by their destination MAC address.
questions.e: A hub copies every bit out of every other port; it does not look at addresses.

questions.q: True or false: A router interface has both an IP address and a MAC address.
questions.e: It is a network-layer device that also sits on a link.

questions.q: A network built with a hub is physically a ___ but behaves logically like a ___.
questions.e: Cables form a star around the hub, but every station hears every transmission, like a bus.

questions.q: True or false: A switch with 8 connected ports creates 8 collision domains but only 1 broadcast domain.
questions.e: Switches split collision domains; routers and VLANs split broadcast domains.

questions.q: Which device (or feature) separates broadcast domains?
questions.e: Broadcasts stop at a router interface; VLANs make separate broadcast domains on one switch.

questions.q: Redundant links between switches without spanning tree cause…
questions.e: Broadcasts circulate endlessly around the loop.

questions.q: True or false: Spanning tree removes loops by logically blocking some ports while keeping the physical links.
questions.e: Blocked links stay as backups.

questions.q: A VLAN creates a separate…
questions.e: VLANs are broadcast domains defined in software.

questions.q: True or false: Moving a station to another VLAN requires rewiring the building.
questions.e: Membership is changed in software.

questions.q: The Internet's network layer uses…
questions.e: Each datagram is routed independently, with no network-layer handshake.

questions.q: True or false: In datagram switching, packets of one message can arrive out of order.
questions.e: They may take different paths.

questions.q: Which address is invalid?
questions.e: 300 is larger than 255, so it cannot be an octet.
Limited broadcast stays on the local network; a directed broadcast targets all hosts of a named network.

questions.q: Host 10.1.1.5/24 sends to 10.1.2.9. Whose MAC address does it ask for with ARP?
questions.e: The destination is on another network, so the frame goes to the router.

questions.q: NAT mainly…
o: Lets many private hosts share a public IP address
questions.e: It translates private addresses to a public one using a table.

questions.q: True or false: Every router decrements TTL and recomputes the header checksum.
questions.e: TTL changes, so the header checksum must be recomputed.

questions.q: True or false: Fragments are reassembled by each router along the path.
questions.e: Only the destination reassembles them.

questions.q: True or false: Internet routing is hierarchical because one flat table for every router would be far too large.
questions.e: Autonomous systems split the problem.

questions.q: True or false: The shortest path always has the fewest hops.
questions.e: It has the least total cost; a longer path can be cheaper.

questions.q: A router at the edge of an AS that connects it to a neighbouring AS runs…
o: An interior protocol inside and BGP outside
questions.e: Border routers run both.

questions.q: True or false: An autonomous system is a group of networks under one administration with a unique AS number.
questions.e: That is the definition.

questions.q: Which four values identify one TCP connection?
o: Source IP, destination IP, source MAC, destination MAC
Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port
Source port, destination port, sequence number, ACK
Destination IP and destination port only
questions.e: Different source ports let one client open several connections to the same server.

questions.q: True or false: TCP sequence numbers count segments, not bytes.
questions.e: They number bytes; each segment's number is the number of its first byte.

questions.q: True or false: The receive window (rwnd) tells the sender how many bytes it may send before waiting for an acknowledgment.
questions.e: That is how TCP does flow control.

questions.q: Which question does DNS answer?
o: Which MAC belongs to an IP?
Which IP address belongs to this host name?
Which port does a process use?
questions.e: DNS maps names to IP addresses (ARP maps IP to MAC).

questions.q: True or false: The root of the DNS tree has an empty label, written as a dot.
questions.e: That is why an FQDN ends with a dot.

questions.q: True or false: Two children of the same node can have the same label.
questions.e: Children of one node must have different labels; that keeps names unique.

questions.q: A domain is…
o: A subtree of the domain name space
questions.e: The domain name is the name of the node at the top of that subtree.

questions.q: Who completes a PQDN?
o: The DNS resolver on the client
questions.e: The resolver adds the missing suffix; only an FQDN can be mapped to an address.

questions.q: True or false: DNS is a centralized database stored on one server.
questions.e: It is distributed and hierarchical, so there is no single point of failure.

questions.q: True or false: Cached DNS answers carry a time-to-live so out-of-date mappings expire.
questions.e: TTL limits how long an answer is reused.

questions.q: Given eight computers connected to a single switch configured with VLAN 10 (A, B, C), VLAN 20 (D, E, F), and VLAN 30 (G, H), how many broadcast domains exist?
o: 1 broadcast domain, because all computers are connected to the same physical switch.
3 broadcast domains, corresponding to VLAN 10, VLAN 20, and VLAN 30.
8 broadcast domains, because each computer operates in its own isolated domain.
4 broadcast domains, including a native management VLAN.
questions.e: One broadcast domain per VLAN: 3. Without VLANs the switch would be 1 broadcast domain. (8 would be the number of collision domains, one per port.)

questions.q: If computer A (belonging to VLAN 10) sends an Ethernet broadcast across the switch, which other computers will receive the broadcast?
o: All seven other computers (B, C, D, E, F, G, and H) connected to the switch.
Only computers D, E, and F, because they share the same physical port group.
Only computers B and C, since A's incoming port is excluded from flooding within VLAN 10.
No other computers, because Layer 2 switches drop all broadcast traffic by default.
questions.e: A broadcast is flooded only to ports in the same VLAN, and never back out the port it arrived on: B and C.

questions.q: Can computer A communicate directly with computer D using only Layer 2 switching?
o: Yes, because both computers are plugged into the exact same physical switch.
Yes, provided that the switch ports are configured in trunking mode.
No, because A belongs to VLAN 10 while D belongs to VLAN 20, and Layer 2 switching keeps these VLANs separate.
No, unless both computers share the exact same MAC address table entry.
questions.e: Different VLANs = different broadcast domains. Traffic between them needs a router (layer 3). A trunk only carries several VLANs between switches; it doesn't join them.

questions.q: A company connects its office in Riyadh to its office in Dammam (about 400 km away) so employees can share files and printers. What type of network is this?
o: LAN, because only one company owns it.
MAN, because both offices are in Saudi Arabia.
WAN, because it connects sites in different cities over a long distance.
PAN, because only employees use it.
questions.e: Size decides the type: LAN = a building or campus, MAN = one city, WAN = across cities or countries. Riyadh to Dammam spans two cities, so it is a WAN. Ownership doesn't decide it.

questions.q: Two branch offices use a link on which both sides can send and receive at the same moment, like a telephone call. What is this data flow mode?
questions.e: Full-duplex = both directions at the same time (telephone). Half-duplex = both directions but one at a time (walkie-talkie). Simplex = one direction only (keyboard). Multipoint describes how many devices share a link, not the direction.

questions.q: In byte-oriented framing, the data contains a byte with the same pattern as the flag. What does the sender do?
o: Discards the frame and sends a NAK.
Inserts an escape (ESC) byte before it (byte stuffing).
Inserts a 0 after five consecutive 1s (bit stuffing).
Changes the flag to a different pattern.
questions.e: Byte stuffing: an ESC byte goes in front of any flag or ESC pattern in the data, and the receiver removes it. Inserting a 0 after five 1s is bit stuffing, used in bit-oriented framing.

questions.q: A code has a minimum Hamming distance of 4. How many bit errors can it guarantee to DETECT?
questions.e: To detect s errors you need d<sub>min</sub> = s + 1, so s = 4 − 1 = 3. (To correct t errors you need d<sub>min</sub> = 2t + 1, so this code corrects only 1.)

questions.q: A frame arrives with destination address 4A:30:10:21:10:1A. What type of address is it?
o: Unicast, because the second hex digit of the first byte is even.
Multicast, because the address starts with 4.
Broadcast, because it contains the digit A.
Multicast, because the last byte is odd.
questions.e: Look at the least significant bit of the first byte: 4A = 0100 1010, last bit 0 → unicast. If it were 1, it would be multicast. Broadcast is all Fs.

questions.q: Which device can join two LAN segments and forward a frame only to the segment where the destination MAC address is?
questions.e: A switch has a MAC table and filters: it forwards only out of the port where the destination was learned. Hubs and repeaters work at layer 1 and copy bits to every port.

questions.q: Why does a new computer send its DHCPDISCOVER message as a broadcast?
o: Because DHCP only works with broadcasts.
Because it does not yet have an IP address and does not know the DHCP server's address.
To find the default gateway's MAC address.
To ask the DNS server for its name.
questions.e: Before DHCP the client has no IP and doesn't know where the server is, so it uses source 0.0.0.0 and destination 255.255.255.255. Finding a MAC address is ARP's job.

questions.q: RIP is an example of which routing approach, and what metric does it use?
questions.e: RIP = distance vector with hop count (maximum 15; 16 = unreachable). OSPF is link state (Dijkstra); BGP is path vector between autonomous systems.

questions.q: A video-calling application must keep delay low and can tolerate a few lost packets. Which transport protocol suits it?
o: TCP, because it retransmits every lost segment.
UDP, because it has no handshake or retransmission delay.
Neither: video calls use IP directly.
questions.e: Real-time audio and video prefer UDP: a retransmitted packet would arrive too late to play. File transfer, email and the web need TCP's reliability.

questions.q: A local DNS server answers a repeated query for www.psu.edu.sa from its cache. What stops it from using that answer forever?
o: The root server deletes it every hour.
Each cached record has a Time-To-Live (TTL); it is removed when the TTL expires.
The client sends an ARP request to refresh it.
Caching is not allowed in DNS.
questions.e: Cached records carry a TTL set by the authoritative server. When it runs out the entry is dropped, and the next query goes to the hierarchy again.

questions.q: The transport layer is responsible for ___ delivery.
questions.e: Data link = node-to-node (hop), network = host-to-host, transport = process-to-process (uses port numbers to reach the right application).

questions.q: A socket address is the combination of:
questions.e: Socket address = IP address (finds the host) + port number (finds the process on that host).

questions.q: How many bits is a port number?
questions.e: Port numbers are 16 bits → 0 to 65,535.

questions.q: Port number 53 falls in which range?
questions.e: 0–1023 well-known (assigned by ICANN), 1024–49,151 registered, 49,152–65,535 dynamic (ephemeral). 53 = DNS.

questions.q: Port number 8080 falls in which range?
questions.e: 8080 is between 1024 and 49,151 → registered.

questions.q: Port number 52,100 falls in which range?
questions.e: Anything from 49,152 to 65,535 is dynamic/ephemeral — typically picked by the client.

questions.q: Which statement about client/server port numbers is correct?
o: Server uses an ephemeral port, client a well-known port
Client uses an ephemeral port, server a well-known port
questions.e: The server listens on a well-known port so clients can find it; the client picks a temporary (ephemeral) port.

questions.q: Multiplexing and demultiplexing happen at:
questions.e: Sender: many processes → one transport layer (many-to-one = multiplexing). Receiver: one transport layer → the correct process by port (one-to-many = demultiplexing).

questions.q: Which service–port pair is correct?
questions.e: SMTP 25, TELNET 23, SSH 22, DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 20/21, TFTP 69, SNMP 161/162, POP3 110.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a transport-layer duty?
questions.e: Routing is the network layer’s job.

questions.q: Why are port addresses only 16 bits while IP addresses are 32 bits?
o: Ports only need to identify processes within one host
questions.e: A port only has to be unique inside one host (per protocol), so a much smaller space is enough. IP addresses must be unique across the whole Internet.

questions.q: The UDP header is:
questions.e: UDP header = 4 fields × 2 bytes = 8 bytes, fixed.

questions.q: Which set lists the UDP header fields?
o: Source port, destination port, sequence number, checksum
Source port, destination port, total length, checksum
Source port, destination port, HLEN, window
Source IP, destination IP, length, checksum
questions.e: UDP: source port (16) · destination port (16) · total length (16) · checksum (16).

questions.q: A UDP header in hex is CB84 000D 001C 001C. The packet is travelling:
questions.e: Destination port 13 is well-known (Daytime) and source port 52,100 is ephemeral → client → server.

questions.q: In IPv4, the UDP checksum is:
o: Optional (all 0s means it was not computed)
questions.e: UDP checksum is optional in IPv4 (field = all 0s if not used). TCP checksum is mandatory.

questions.q: The UDP/TCP checksum pseudoheader includes:
o: Source IP, destination IP, protocol and UDP length
questions.e: Pseudoheader = source IP, destination IP, zeros, protocol (17 for UDP), UDP total length. It protects against delivery to the wrong host.

questions.q: What is the value of the protocol field in the IP header when it carries UDP?
questions.e: UDP = 17, TCP = 6, ICMP = 1, OSPF = 89.

questions.q: Which application is the best fit for UDP?
o: Sending an email with an attachment
questions.e: DNS: a small request and reply, speed matters, the app can just ask again. Also: SNMP, TFTP, RIP, DHCP, real-time audio/video.

questions.q: UDP is best described as:
questions.e: UDP keeps message boundaries (one message = one datagram), has no connection setup, and does no retransmission.

questions.q: Which of these does UDP provide?
questions.e: UDP gives only error detection (checksum). A corrupted datagram is silently discarded, not retransmitted.

questions.q: TCP is:
questions.e: TCP sets up a connection, numbers bytes, retransmits, and data flows both ways at the same time.

questions.q: The size of the TCP header is:
questions.e: 20 bytes without options, up to 60 with 40 bytes of options.

questions.q: Which HLEN value can never appear in a valid TCP header?
questions.e: 0100 = 4 × 4 = 16 bytes, but the minimum header is 20 bytes (HLEN = 5). 1111 = 60 bytes (maximum).

questions.q: A TCP header dump in hex: 05320017 00000001 00000000 500207FF 00000000 Which control flag is set, and what does that mean?
questions.e: 0x5002 → HLEN 0101 | reserved 000000 | flags 000010. Flag order URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN → SYN. Destination port 23 = TELNET, so a client is asking a TELNET server to connect.

questions.q: Which flag aborts (resets) a connection?
questions.e: RST resets / refuses a connection. FIN closes it normally.

questions.q: Which flag asks the receiver to deliver data to the application right away instead of waiting for the buffer to fill?
questions.e: PSH = push. URG marks urgent data, using the urgent pointer.

questions.q: The urgent pointer field is valid only if:
questions.e: The urgent pointer is used only when URG = 1. It gives the end of the urgent data.

questions.q: The sequence-number field of a TCP segment holds:
o: The number of the first data byte in that segment
The number of the last byte received
The number of the next byte expected
questions.e: TCP numbers bytes, not segments. Seq = the number of the first byte in the segment. (The next byte expected is the ACK number.)

questions.q: The acknowledgment number in TCP is:
o: The number of the last byte received
The number of the next byte expected (cumulative)
questions.e: TCP ACKs are cumulative: ack = number of the next byte the receiver expects.

questions.q: The initial sequence number (ISN) is:
questions.e: The ISN is random, so old duplicate segments and attackers can’t easily guess sequence numbers. The seq field is 32 bits.

questions.q: The window-size field is 16 bits, so the maximum window is:
questions.e: 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535 bytes (without the window-scale option).

questions.q: Unlike UDP, the TCP checksum is:
questions.e: TCP checksum is mandatory and covers pseudoheader + header + data.

questions.q: Which segment carries no data but still consumes ONE sequence number?
questions.e: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. A pure ACK consumes none.

questions.q: A pure ACK segment (no data):
questions.e: It still carries a seq number in the header, but doesn’t consume one, so the next data segment reuses the same seq.

questions.q: In the 3-way handshake, the flags of the 3 segments are, in order:
questions.e: Client SYN → server SYN + ACK → client ACK.

questions.q: A SYN-flooding attack:
o: Sends many FIN segments to close connections
Sends many SYNs with fake source IPs so the server reserves resources for half-open connections
Floods the server with data segments
questions.e: It’s a denial-of-service attack. Defences: SYN cookies, limiting half-open connections, filtering fake addresses.

questions.q: The server does a ___ open and the client does an ___ open.
questions.e: The server does a passive open (LISTEN); the client does an active open by sending the SYN.

questions.q: Half-close means:
o: Both sides stop at the same time
One side stops sending data but can still receive
questions.e: E.g. the client sends FIN after uploading but keeps receiving the server’s data. This is 4-way termination: FIN, ACK, (data…), FIN, ACK.

questions.q: How long does a TCP endpoint stay in the TIME-WAIT state?
questions.e: 2 MSL: it can resend the last ACK if it is lost, and old duplicates die out before a new connection reuses the same socket pair.

questions.q: A server that is waiting for connection requests is in state:
questions.e: Passive open → LISTEN. Client after sending SYN → SYN-SENT.

questions.q: The client has sent FIN and received its ACK, but hasn’t yet received the server’s FIN. Its state is:
questions.e: FIN-WAIT-1 (FIN sent) → ACK received → FIN-WAIT-2 → server FIN received & ACKed → TIME-WAIT.

questions.q: The server has received the client’s FIN and acknowledged it, but hasn’t sent its own FIN yet. Its state is:
questions.e: Server: CLOSE-WAIT → sends FIN → LAST-ACK → gets ACK → CLOSED.

questions.q: Which segment consumes a sequence number when it carries no data?
questions.e: FIN (like SYN) consumes one sequence number.

questions.q: Flow control in TCP is mainly done using:
questions.e: The receiver advertises rwnd so the sender can’t overflow the receiver’s buffer.

questions.q: Silly window syndrome caused by the SENDER is solved by:
questions.e: Nagle: send the first piece, then gather data until an ACK arrives or a full segment is ready.

questions.q: Silly window syndrome caused by the RECEIVER is solved by:
questions.e: Clark: advertise a zero window until there’s room for a full segment or half the buffer is free. Or delay the ACK.

questions.q: The three tools TCP uses for error control are:
questions.e: A corrupted segment is detected by the checksum and dropped. A missing ACK leads to a time-out (or 3 duplicate ACKs) and a retransmission.

questions.q: Fast retransmission is triggered when the sender receives:
questions.e: 3 duplicate ACKs (4 identical ACKs in total) → resend the missing segment without waiting for the RTO.

questions.q: A receiver gets an out-of-order segment (a gap is detected). It:
o: Stores it and immediately sends an ACK with the next expected byte (a duplicate ACK)
questions.e: Modern TCP stores out-of-order segments, but the ACK still names the first missing byte, which creates the duplicate ACKs that trigger fast retransmit.

questions.q: A receiver with no data to send gets an in-order segment and the previous one was already ACKed. It:
o: Delays the ACK until another segment arrives or about 500 ms pass
questions.e: The delayed-ACK rule cuts down on ACK traffic.

questions.q: The ACK for segment 1 is lost, but the ACK for segment 2 arrives before the timer for segment 1 expires. What happens?
o: Nothing — the cumulative ACK covers both segments
questions.e: Cumulative ACKs mean a lost ACK is often harmless.

questions.q: Can a TCP receiver shrink its window (move the right edge to the left)?
o: No — shrinking is strongly discouraged / not allowed
questions.e: The right wall shouldn’t move left, because the sender may already have sent bytes into that space. The receiver can close the window (rwnd = 0) instead.

questions.q: In slow start, cwnd grows:
questions.e: +1 MSS per ACK → doubles each RTT, until it reaches ssthresh.

questions.q: In congestion avoidance, cwnd grows:
questions.e: Additive increase. Together with halving on loss (multiplicative decrease) this is AIMD.

questions.q: In TCP Reno, 3 duplicate ACKs arrive. TCP:
o: Sets cwnd = 1 and starts slow start
Sets ssthresh = cwnd/2 and enters fast recovery (doesn’t drop to 1)
questions.e: 3 duplicate ACKs mean light congestion (later segments are still getting through) → fast recovery. A time-out means heavy congestion → cwnd = 1.

questions.q: Which event is treated as the stronger sign of congestion?
questions.e: A time-out means nothing is getting through, so TCP reacts most strongly (cwnd = 1).

questions.q: Karn’s algorithm says:
o: Don’t use the RTT of a retransmitted segment when updating RTTs
Use a fixed RTO of 1 s
questions.e: When a segment was retransmitted, you can’t tell which copy the ACK is for. Ignore that sample and use exponential backoff for the RTO.

questions.q: The persistence timer is used to:
o: Prevent deadlock after the receiver advertises a zero window (send probes)
questions.e: If the ACK that reopens the window is lost, both sides would wait forever. Probes avoid that.

questions.q: Which timer stops a long-idle connection from staying open forever (e.g. after the client crashes)?
questions.e: Keepalive: after a long idle time (often 2 hours) send probes; if there’s no response, close the connection.

questions.q: Which are TCP’s four timers?
questions.e: Retransmission (RTO) · persistence · keepalive · TIME-WAIT (2 MSL).

questions.q: Stop-and-Wait uses sequence numbers:
questions.e: With one outstanding packet, you only need to tell “new” from “duplicate” → modulo 2.

questions.q: The receive-window size in Go-Back-N is:
questions.e: GBN receiver accepts only the next expected packet. In SR the receive window = send window = 2ᵐ⁻¹.

questions.q: Go-Back-N: packets 0–6 are sent and packet 3 is lost. When packet 3’s timer expires, the sender resends:
questions.e: GBN resends every outstanding packet from the lost one on. (The receiver threw away 4–6.)

questions.q: Selective Repeat: packets 0–6 are sent and packet 3 is lost. When packet 3’s timer expires, the sender resends:
questions.e: SR buffers out-of-order packets and resends only the lost one.

questions.q: In Go-Back-N, the sender receives an ACK with ackNo = 5. This means:
o: Packets up to 4 arrived; packet 5 is expected next
questions.e: GBN ACKs are cumulative and give the next expected packet.

questions.q: Stop-and-Wait: the ACK is lost, the sender times out and resends. The receiver:
o: Delivers the duplicate to the application
Spots the duplicate by its sequence number, discards it, and resends the ACK
questions.e: That’s why sequence numbers are needed even in Stop-and-Wait.

questions.q: Why must the SR window be at most 2ᵐ⁻¹?
o: So that new and retransmitted packets with the same seq number can’t be confused when all ACKs are lost
questions.e: A bigger window lets the receiver’s window wrap around and accept an old duplicate as new data.
